stories.title: Kinahan loses final appeal, set to face trial in Ireland
stories.summary: Daniel Kinahan, one of the leaders of the Kinahan Organised Crime Group, has lost his final appeal in Dubai and is to be sent home to face trial here. An Garda Síochána, the Defence Forces and the Departments of Justice and Foreign Affairs are making preparations to extradite him, but no timeline has been finalised for his return. He will remain in custody in Dubai until he is handed over to the gardaí which is expected in the next six weeks. Mr Kinahan could have consented to his extradition but instead he fought against it for the past three months, a fight he has now lost.

stories.title: EU Commissioner accepts fisheries facing challenges
stories.summary: Minister for the Marine Martin Heydon and the EU Fisheries Commissioner Costas Kadis have responded to warnings from two of the country's leading fishing organisations that the sector is in crisis and will not survive without urgent support from the Government and EU. They were speaking as fisheries ministers from 27 EU states gather in Cork for an informal meeting, as part of Ireland's Presidency of the Council of the EU. Ireland's fishery and seafood sector employs 10,000 people directly, another 7,000 indirectly and is worth €1.25bn to the Irish economy every year. Earlier this month, a report to Marine Minister Timmy Dooley by consultant Kieran Mulvey, found the sector is facing an existential threat.

stories.title: AIB posts half year profits of €939m, new lending up 10%
stories.summary: AIB has reported profits after tax of €939m for the six months to the end of June, a 1.3% increase on the €927m it reported the same time last year. The bank said it had entered the second half of the year with confidence. AIB said its gross loans rose by 3% to €74.5 billion from the end of last year, while total new lending increased by 10% to €7.5 billion from €6.9 billion the same time last year. Its new mortgage lending in Ireland rose to €2 billion from €1.9 billion in the first half of last year, which resulted in a mortgage market share of 30%.

stories.title: Japan quake toll reaches 13 as rescue efforts continue
stories.summary: A 7.1-magnitude earthquake killed at least 13 people near the southern Japanese city of Kumamoto, and rescuers are frantically searching for survivors trapped beneath the rubble, Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said. "Even now, there are people waiting to be rescued, and this is a race against time. We will marshal all available resources on the ground to save and rescue as many people as possible," Ms Takaichi told reporters at her office in Tokyo a day after the quake struck, raising the toll from three deaths reported earlier. The quake knocked out power to thousands of homes and ruptured roads across the region. Eight people were pulled from the rubble of a partially collapsed shopping mall near the city of Kumamoto that was torn apart by an apparent explosion about an hour after earthquake, among them two dead women in their 20s.

stories.title: O'Shea out to savour Croke Park joy for Kerry this year
stories.summary: The emotions of All-Ireland final defeat have lingered in Kerry throughout the week, but women's football captain Síofra O'Shea insists that the defeat to Mayo in the men's decider will have no bearing on their own preparations. Just days after that loss, O'Shea says that her side have remained firmly focused on their own challenge as they prepare to take on Galway in this Sunday's TG4 All-Ireland SFC final at Croke Park. Speaking at a media day ahead of the finals at GAA HQ, O'Shea revealed that the squad had already prepared mentally for whatever unfolded regarding the Sam Maguire outcome with their sports psychologist encouraging the players to stay committed to their own journey. "I think our psychologist is great, and we had a good meeting with her last Friday before the men's final just about how we're sticking with our own game no matter what happens," O'Shea explained.

stories.summary: Patrick McEleney has taken charge of Finn Harps on an interim basis for the rest of the season after retiring from playing. Patrick McEleney, still just 33, had been playing with Ballymena United in the Northern Ireland Premiership before calling time on that career to take up this Harps role. He did serve as part of the Derry City coaching staff that secured a second-place finish in the 2025 League of Ireland Premier Division and was part of the interim coaching staff at Ballymena last season.

stories.title: Schmidt back in Irish rugby with Ulster development role
stories.summary: Ulster Rugby has confirmed the appointment of former Ireland boss Joe Schmidt as a coach development officer with the province. Schmidt led Ireland to three Six Nations titles, including a Grand Slam, between 2013 and 2019 following on from a successful spell with Leinster, where he guided the team to two Heineken Cup successes. He stepped away from coaching for a period before returning to an assistant role with his native New Zealand, helping them to reach the 2023 World Cup final. The 60-year-old spent the last two years as head coach of the Wallabies before making way for former Ulster boss Les Kiss earlier this month.

stories.title: 100 Buildings: A Modernist surprise on the streets of Dungarvan
stories.summary: The Dungarvan Further Education and Training Centre is an unexpected Modern Movement gem in the suburbs of Dungarvan, County Waterford, on a corner site bounded by Wolfe Tone Road and O'Connell Street. If walking by, do look closer at the entrance for a sign of its past. In 1899, technical schools were set up in Ireland to provide more practical vocational training. The 1930 Vocational Education Act gave local councils the funds to develop technical education further with the building of bespoke vocational schools. Many charged nominal fees, which were small compared to the cost of going to secondary school. Free secondary school education was not available until 1967. In 1933, the Waterford County Surveyor, John Kingston Bowen (1888–1944), was tasked with designing a vocational school for Dungarvan. Scoil na gCeárd (translates to vocational school). The school building was officially opened on the 5th of April 1939, with Thomas Derrig (1897–1956), Minister for Education, in attendance. John was brother to Richard Bowen, County Surveyor for Kilkenny, who designed the Padmore and Barnes Boot Factory. The Waterford County VEC amalgamated with Wexford in 2011 and today the building is run by Dungarvan Further Education and Training Centre, which still provides training for adults across Waterford and Wexford. The school is a well-proportioned five-bay, two-storey, flat-roofed building in the International Style, with a single-bay, two-storey advanced entrance bay and a two-storey return. The entrance is sheltered by a concrete canopy, over which there is a rendered panel with raised lettering spelling out 'Scoil na gCeárd' in beautiful Gaelic letterform. The painted rendered walls give the building a clean appearance, and the low rendered boundary wall, piers, and pedestrian gate (blocked) still remain. All the windows were unfortunately replaced by uPVC casement windows in the early nineties. It is set back from the road, and its geometric form and massing are softened by mature trees.

According to the study from EU Agency Eurofound, Ireland is ahead of the EU average of 20% and has experienced a 20 percentage point increase in remote working between 2015 and 2024. Luxembourg leads the way on 41%, followed closely by the Netherlands and Sweden. At the other end of the scale, just 4% of workers in Romania engaged in remote working in 2024, while the figure was just 6% in Italy.

stories.title: US Senate advances Russia sanctions as Zelensky visits
stories.summary: The US Senate advanced sweeping Russian energy sanctions legislation as Ukrainian President ⁠Volodymyr Zelensky visited the Capitol, seeing the vote as a tribute to the bill's author, the late Senator Lindsey Graham, on the day of his funeral. Mr Graham was among Kyiv's most influential and outspoken allies in Congress in its four-year-old war against Russia, and the bill aims to increase economic pressure on Moscow over its invasion of Ukraine. The tally was 86 to 12 in favour on a procedural vote to advance the bill, which seeks to impose sanctions on Russian officials and authorise stiff tariffs on China, India and other countries to reduce their dependence on Russian oil and gas. Republican President Donald Trump has said he would support the measure, after asking that sanctions on Iran be added, which they have been as the US war against Iran enters its sixth month.

stories.title: Something for the Weekend: Patrick Freyne's cultural picks
stories.summary: When he isn't penning articles for The Irish Times, writer Patrick Freyne is busy publishing acclaimed books. He follows his popular essay collection OK, Let's Do Your Stupid Idea with a debut novel, Experts In A Dying Field, a wryly amusing musical tale inspired by a years spent playing in cult Irish bands like El Diablo and National Prayer Breakfast - read an extract here, and listen to Patrick in conversation with Brendan O'Connor below... I absolutely loved Weapons, directed and written Zach Cregger. Horror is where you find all the interesting indie directors go nowadays, because there are few other places to experiment. So Weapons jumps horrifically from subplot to subplot and character to character in a way that's like Robert Altman’s Short Cuts or Paul Thomas Anderson’s Magnolia or Richard Linklater’s Slacker. That multi-perspective structure ultimately services a weird folk horror story masquerading as a thriller. It’s amazingly well-structured with a brilliant cast including Josh Brolin, Julia Garner, Benedict Wong and veteran character actress Amy Madigan, who was given an Oscar for her trouble. There isn’t a genre alive I don’t feel could be improved by a banjo or some other twanging instrument (grime/classical music/poetry). So I love the explosion of excellent traditional/folk acts like Lisa O’Neil, The Mary Wallopers, Ye Vagabonds, Lankum, Poor Creature and Landless. I am very looking forward to the forthcoming solo record from Lankum's Radie Peat.

stories.title: BTS pull out of Grammys over new Asian pop category
stories.summary: K-pop stars BTS have said they will not submit their music for next year's Grammy Awards, after the Recording Academy in the US introduced a new Asian pop category criticised for restricting the success of regional artists. BTS were widely tipped to be in the running for several of the Grammys' top honours, including Album of the Year, after the South Korean act's comeback album, ARIRANG, became one of this year's best-selling hits. But the seven-member group said they would not enter the contest after the introduction of five new categories, including Best Asian Pop Music Performance. "We have decided not to enter the Grammys this year," BTS members said in coordinated posts on their individual Instagram accounts.

stories.title: I spent 8 days exploring Sri Lanka, here's what I learned
stories.summary: On an eight-day journey through Sri Lanka, courtesy of Intrepid Travel, Deirdre Mullins discovers a country shaped by ritual, resilience and extraordinary generosity. I'm standing at the entrance of a hotel function room, welcomed by the impeccably dressed parents of the bride. I’m wearing baggy fisherman’s trousers and dusty Birkenstocks, and, despite being underdressed for the occasion, they smile, press their palms together and offer ayubowan, a wish for a long life. I’m wedding-crashing in Sri Lanka, but perhaps it’s the only place in the world where you can’t actually crash a wedding; you’re simply welcomed in. We’re ushered towards the bride and groom, who preside over the room like royalty, as if they’ve stepped out of another century. The bride wears an ivory, jewel-studded sari layered with heavy gold necklaces and crowned with an ornate headpiece.

stories.title: EPA warns of drinking water contamination risk
stories.summary: The Environmental Protection Agency has warned that thousands of people could be drinking water from private supplies that are not being monitored for contamination, posing an ongoing risk to public health. The agency is calling on the Department of Housing, Local Government and Heritage to change the law so that all private drinking water supplies must be registered with local authorities and routinely monitored. There are thousands of Small Private Water Supplies providing drinking water from wells and other private sources to schools, crèches, nursing homes, hotels, campsites, sports clubs and other commercial and public premises across Ireland. However, only about 1,600 are registered with local authorities - a requirement if the supplies are to be sampled and monitored to ensure the water is safe to drink.

stories.title: Crews continue to manage flare-ups on Slievenamon
stories.summary: A Status Orange high forest fire risk warning has been extended nationwide until midday next Tuesday, as fire crews continue to manage and monitor flare-ups which have reignited across Slievenamon in Co Tipperary. Acting Senior Assistant Chief Fire Officer at Tipperary Fire and Rescue Service Carol Kennedy said that due to the high temperatures in already burnt ground, it is not unusual for fire lines to reignite. "It was a lot cooler on the ground here today but then the clouds broke because of the recent fires and at the moment it doesn't take a lot to burn what’s on the ground," she said. The wildfire, now in its 10th day, is expected to continue until significant rainfall gets under way.

stories.title: Does a sweary boss make you work harder (or want to quit)?
stories.summary: Analysis: People's reactions to swearing in the workplace depends on what is being said, who is listening and where they live By Alexandros Psychogios, Loughborough University and Dritjon Gruda, Universidade Católica Portuguesa Some people love to swear. In the workplace, some of those people might be in charge. You may have worked with one (or be one) yourself: the team leader who likes to pepper a pep talk with spicy language, or the manager who uses swear words to express themselves in the clearest possible terms. How colleagues respond to colourful language varies. Some might enjoy it, while others are unbothered. It can also be considered a sign of poor leadership, unprofessional – and simply unnecessary. Our research suggests people’s reactions to a sweary boss depend not only on what is being said, but also on who is listening and where they live. We found that there is not a single "correct" way for leaders to communicate. But overall, employees were less satisfied with supervisors who frequently used profanity. So if you’re wondering whether filling meetings with swear words is a good management strategy, it’s probably safer to avoid them.

stories.title: Deadliest year for antisemitic attacks since '94 - report
stories.summary: Last year was the "deadliest" for antisemitic attacks in more than 30 years, according to a report released today by the J7 Large Communities' Task Force Against Antisemitism. The report looked at incidents in Argentina, Australia, Canada, France, Germany, the United Kingdom and the United States, which make up more than 90% of the Jewish diaspora. Twenty people were murdered in antisemitic attacks in Australia, the UK and the US in 2025, making it "the deadliest year for antisemitic attacks in the diaspora ... since the AMIA attack in Buenos Aires in 1994." In December, 15 people were killed in an antisemitic mass shooting at a Hanukkah festival near Australia's Bondi Beach.

stories.title: Geraghty: Mayo mission can inspire 'underdogs' Galway
stories.summary: Perhaps it's the year of the underdog after all. This week, a rampaging Kerry side wear the favourites' tag as their success-starved Connacht foes await in an All-Ireland final in Croke Park. Galway captain Kate Geraghty is looking fairly close to home for inspiration ahead of the Tribeswomen's latest quest to bridge an All-Ireland Women's SFC drought that stretches back to 2004. A mere 22 years? Sure that's nothing in this day and age. The raucous scenes of unbridled delirium witnessed at Headquarters on Sunday of last week proved a recurring talking point at the LGFA's All-Ireland finals launch earlier this week. Mayo men's improbable victory ended 75 years of hurt - and prompted those elsewhere who are overdue a title to nudge their team-mates and wonder 'why not us?'. "They were huge underdogs. Nobody really backed them at all," Geraghty said this week, with our most recent Sam Maguire winners in mind.
